question: Why does an ultrasound probe need a layer of gel against the skin?
answer: Because a thin film of air would reflect almost all the sound back. Sound crosses a boundary well only when both sides resist it similarly, and air is thousands of times less resistant than tissue: about 99.9% bounces at a tissue-air boundary. The same law keeps ultrasound from seeing through air-filled lungs or gassy bowel.
move: A gap of almost nothing can block what a wall of flesh lets through.
ask: What tiny gap between me and something I need is blocking more than a wall would?
reference: Szabo, Diagnostic Ultrasound Imaging: Inside Out, Elsevier Academic Press, 2004
